title: 17 August 2026: BMS demonstrations across the country
author: Editorial Desk
summary: District and State headquarters saw dharnas on long-pending demands.
body:
On **17 August 2026**, BMS units held **nationwide demonstrations** at district headquarters, State headquarters and industrial estates. The programme had been decided by the **Kendriya Karya Samithi** at its meeting in Ranchi and announced in late July. This post sets out the background, the demands, how the day was organised and what it was meant to achieve.

## Background: a year of building pressure

BMS has been raising the same family of issues for some time. Its 21st triennial conference was held in Odisha from 6 to 8 February 2026. On 25 February it observed a "Virodh Diwas", or protest day, with demonstrations in several States, and on 26 February it submitted a memorandum to the Centre citing poor implementation of the labour codes. In a statement before that protest, BMS described the Government's response as lukewarm and inadequate, according to ThePrint. The four Labour Codes had come into force on 21 November 2025, after roughly six years of delay, merging 29 central laws.

The decision for 17 August came at the all-India working committee meeting held in Ranchi from 26 to 28 July 2026, which Organiser's report calls the 161st meeting of the committee. About 150 representatives of States and federations attended. A BMS notice then directed all units to observe 17 August as Demands Day, with dharnas and demonstrations to mount pressure on the Government. A press report of 13 August said the call went to all 28 State units and 42 industrial federations.

## What the programme said

According to BMS's press notes, the call was to demand the **resolution of long-pending problems of workers**. BMS also said that it opposed the **Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code**, which it says contain many anti-worker provisions, and asked the Government to start talks with central trade unions and bring in amendments. Memoranda were to go to the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister and the Labour Minister through district authorities.

## The demands

The BMS release and later reports list the following, grouped here for clarity.

**Pensions and social security**
- Raise the minimum pension under the Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 from Rs 1,000 to Rs 7,500 a month, with dearness relief, and link it to the Ayushman Bharat health scheme.
- Restore the Old Pension Scheme.
- Raise the Employees' State Insurance wage ceiling from Rs 21,000 to Rs 42,000 and the provident fund ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000, so that more workers are covered.

**Wages, bonus and gratuity**
- Pay bonus on full wages and raise the bonus calculation limit, which the release mentions as Rs 7,000.
- Raise gratuity from 15 to 30 days' wages for each year of service and remove the ceiling.
- Set minimum wages by a formula that follows the rising cost of living.

**Scheme and contract workers**
- Raise monthly honoraria of Anganwadi, ASHA, mid-day meal and National Health Mission workers.
- Give equal pay for equal work to contract workers and penalise contractors and manpower agencies that withhold wages.

**Other demands**
- A five-day banking week.
- Fill vacant posts in government services.
- Hold the Indian Labour Conference at an early date.
- Resolve pending problems at Heavy Engineering Corporation, Ranchi, and at the National Textile Corporation mills.

## The scheme workers argument

The release also made a broader argument that deserves attention. BMS says governments should rethink the concept of "scheme workers". It argues that welfare schemes should have a limited lifespan of ten to twelve years and notes that the Anganwadi scheme began in October 1975. It says Anganwadi workers often work more than twelve hours a day yet are not recognised as workers and so fall outside the labour codes. It puts the number of scheme workers at over ten million, most of them skilled, and calls for a new policy and for discussions with central trade unions on their future.

## What happened on the day

Reports describe demonstrations in many places. In Delhi, thousands of BMS workers from the Delhi Pradesh unit gathered at Jantar Mantar, and a delegation met the Labour Secretary in the Ministry of Labour and Employment and handed over a memorandum addressed to Dr Mansukh Mandaviya, asking for time-bound consideration of eleven demands. Speakers named in the report included B. Surendran, the national organisation secretary, who spoke on pension and the Codes. Press headlines also pointed to programmes in Nagpur and Shimla. No independent count of turnout across the country is available, and figures given by organisers should be read as organisers' estimates.

## What a Demands Day is for

Memoranda handed to local officials reach the Government through the administrative chain, so each district submission is a recorded demand. The size of the turnout also sends a political signal. For BMS, which seeks to be firm but constructive, such a day lies between a strike and a quiet representation. Notably, BMS did not join the 9 July 2025 nationwide strike called by other central unions over the Labour Codes, saying that it considered it politically motivated, according to a press headline of that time; its own method is demonstration and dialogue.

## What followed

On 1 September 2026, BMS reported meetings with the Union Labour Minister and the Union Textile Minister. The Labour Minister meeting, in BMS's headline, ended with the Government giving an assurance of early amendments; the page gives no details. These meetings are the subject of the next post in this series.

## What to watch next

- Whether the Labour Ministry issues any reply on the eleven demands, and on what timetable.
- Whether the Government calls an Indian Labour Conference, the tripartite forum BMS has asked for.
- Whether amendments to the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code are proposed, and how State rules treat the same points.
- Whether pension and wage-ceiling demands, which carry a financial cost, appear in the next Budget.
